# Table of Contents

# 1\. Executive Summary

This document defines Chapter 4 - Backend System Architecture for iPOMS. Where Chapters 1-3 defined the visual identity, the reusable component library, and the screen-by-screen blueprint of the application, Chapter 4 defines the invisible layer between the UI and the code: how data is stored, how screens communicate with the backend, and how business rules actually execute.

This chapter is written for developers and AI-assisted development tools (Claude Code, Cursor AI), not for end users - no iPOMS user will ever see this document, but every screen frozen in Chapter 3 depends on the decisions made here.

This is a living document: Section 4.1 (Overall Backend Architecture) has been discussed in depth and its foundational decisions are frozen below. Sections 4.2 through 4.12 are scoped but not yet designed, and will be added to this specification section by section, following the same process used for the Chapter 3 screens.

# 2\. Purpose of Chapter 4

Chapter 4 answers one question: how will the entire iPOMS system work behind the scenes? It exists so that, before a single line of code is written, every architectural decision - collections, APIs, authentication, relationships, security, search, import - is already made, the same way an architect draws rooms, kitchen, bathroom, and doors before construction begins.

The explicit motivation is AI-assisted development: when Claude Code or Cursor AI later asks "where should I save Daily Tracker data?" or "where should Login verify a password?", this chapter provides the answer directly (daily_tracker collection; users collection) instead of leaving the AI to guess or invent its own structure.

# 3\. Chapter 4 Structure

Chapter 4 is divided into twelve sections. Deliberately, the chapter does not begin with the database - many developers jump straight to "create the database," which is the wrong starting point. The system's overall behaviour (Section 4.1) is defined first, and only then does the chapter decide how data should be stored.

| **Section** | **Title**                    | **Purpose**                                                                |
| ----------- | ---------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 4.1         | Overall Backend Architecture | Complete system flow - the master blueprint every other section depends on |

This document develops Section 4.1 in full. Sections 4.2-4.12 remain scoped placeholders pending their own design sessions (see Section 19, Deferred / Out of Scope).

# 4\. The iPOMS System Model

Before any technical detail, the architecture was explained using a simple analogy - iPOMS as a human body - to make sure the underlying concepts were clear regardless of technical background:

| **Body Part** | **System Layer**               | **Role**                                                                 |
| ------------- | ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Brain         | Business Rules (Backend Logic) | Duplicate detection, auto-save, role permissions, dashboard calculations |
| Heart         | MongoDB Database               | Stores everything, like memory                                           |
| Eyes          | Frontend                       | The screens already designed - Login, Dashboard, Daily Tracker, Reports  |
| Hands         | API                            | The messenger - the frontend asks, the backend replies                   |

Without a backend, typing "Infosys" into the Daily Tracker goes nowhere - nothing is storing it. With a backend, Daily Tracker → Backend → MongoDB → Saved Forever, and the data is still there the next time the coordinator opens the screen.

| **Frontend Does**  | **Backend Does** |
| ------------------ | ---------------- |
| Shows screens      | Makes decisions  |
| Accepts typing     | Validates        |
| Displays tables    | Reads database   |
| Displays dashboard | Calculates KPIs  |
| Displays report    | Generates report |
| Shows login        | Authenticates    |

# 5\. Illustrative Data Flows

The following short flows illustrate how frontend, API, backend logic, and MongoDB interact for operations already defined in Chapters 2 and 3:

- Login: Login Button → API → Backend checks the users collection (email, password, role) → Backend replies Yes, Role = Coordinator → Frontend opens the Coordinator Dashboard. The frontend never checks passwords itself - the backend always does.
- Search Company: typing "INF" → API → Backend searches MongoDB → returns Infosys, Infoziant, Infinite → Frontend displays the three results.
- Save (Daily Tracker): Save → API → Backend validates → stores in MongoDB → returns "Saved Successfully" → Frontend shows a save confirmation.
- Dashboard KPI: opening the dashboard asks the backend "Today's Calls?" → the backend counts Daily Tracker records (e.g. 50) → returns the count → the frontend displays "Today's Calls: 50".
- Generate Report: Generate Weekly Report → backend reads Daily Tracker, Weekly Tracker, Daily Leads, and Metadata → calculates KPIs → creates the report → returns a PDF → the frontend offers it for download.

# 6\. Recommended Technology Stack

| **Purpose**             | **Tool**                                             |
| ----------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| Frontend                | Next.js + Tailwind CSS                               |
| Backend Runtime         | Next.js API Routes (or Route Handlers)               |
| Database                | MongoDB                                              |
| ORM / Database Helper   | Mongoose                                             |
| Authentication          | NextAuth / Auth.js (or a custom JWT-based approach)  |
| File Upload             | ExcelJS + Multer (or native Next.js upload handling) |
| Charts                  | Recharts                                             |
| PDF Reports             | jsPDF / pdf-lib, depending on report needs           |
| AI-Assisted Development | Claude Code + Cursor AI                              |

A separate backend framework (e.g. Spring Boot, Node/Express as a standalone service) is not recommended unless the project grows substantially larger - Next.js can serve both the frontend and the backend APIs for iPOMS, which keeps deployment and maintenance simpler for a system of this scale.

# 7\. How Everything Connects

The master wiring diagram for Section 4.1: the User interacts with the Next.js Frontend, which communicates over API requests with the Next.js Backend (Business Logic). The backend logic layer is composed of Authentication, Business Rules, and Report Logic, all of which read from and write to the MongoDB Database - organized into collections such as Users, Companies, Daily Tracker, and Weekly Tracker, which in turn feed Reports & Dashboards.

This chapter exists to answer exactly the questions this diagram raises: where is the data stored, who is allowed to access it, how do screens communicate, which module supplies data to another, how are duplicates prevented, how are dashboards and reports generated, and how does the application stay fast as records grow into the thousands. None of this is visible to users, but every screen designed in Chapters 1-3 depends on it.

# 8\. Section 4.1 - Foundational Decisions

Before drawing the complete backend architecture, four business questions were asked and answered. These decisions shape every technical choice that follows.

## 8.1 Application Access - Question 1

Decision: iPOMS is used both inside the company office and, in future, over the internet (Option C). It is built primarily for Infoziant's own coordinators, Team Leaders, and Director/CEO, but a further dashboard is also planned for Training & Placement Officers based at partner colleges - meaning the application must support external, internet-based access from the outset, not just an internal office network.

## 8.2 Concurrent Users - Question 2

Decision: approximately 20 coordinators use the system in total, with realistic simultaneous logins of around 5 users at any given moment (login times naturally spread across the morning - 10:00, 10:15, 10:17, 10:30, 11:00, etc.), never a simultaneous spike of all 20. This workload is comfortably within what MongoDB and Next.js can handle; the architecture would remain sound even at 50-100 simultaneous users.

## 8.3 File Storage - Question 3

Decision - a clean separation between database records and files:

- Stored in MongoDB: user information, a profile-photo reference, company data, HR data.
- Stored as files (not in MongoDB): company logos, college logos, imported Excel files (temporarily, while processing), and generated PDF reports - PDFs are downloaded directly to the user's own computer rather than retained permanently on the server.

## 8.4 Future Growth - Question 4

Decision: iPOMS Version 1 supports only Infoziant as a single organization - no multiple branches and no multi-tenant SaaS model in this version. This keeps Version 1 focused, while the broader architectural recommendation (see Section 9) is still to make a few foundational choices now that would not need to be rebuilt if the platform grows later.

# 9\. Clarifying a Common Misconception: API vs. Internet

A key clarification raised during this discussion: API does not mean "the internet." An API is simply the communication mechanism between the frontend and the backend - it runs whether the application is used on an internal office network or over the public internet. Every meaningful operation in iPOMS - Login, Search Company, Import Contacts, Save Tracker, Generate Report - goes through an API call to the backend; this is normal and expected, not something reserved for internet-facing features.

# 10\. Daily Tracker Case Studies - When Do API and MongoDB Actually Run?

Three concrete Daily Tracker scenarios were walked through to clarify exactly when the API and MongoDB get involved, since the coordinator's real workflow (bulk-importing 30-40 contacts, receiving Team Leader assignments) does not involve typing and saving one row at a time.

## 10.1 Case 1 - Importing Contacts from Metadata

Selecting 40 contacts in the Master Company Database and clicking Import to Daily Tracker sends one bulk API request, not 40 separate ones. The backend checks that the contacts exist, confirms the user is permitted to import them, checks for duplicates, and MongoDB stores all 40 records in a single operation - Import 40 Contacts → One API Request → One Backend Validation → MongoDB → 40 Records Saved. This is fast precisely because it is one round trip, not forty.

## 10.2 Case 2 - Team Leader Assigned Contacts

When a Team Leader assigns 15 contacts, those contacts do not come from Excel or from memory - they are already stored in MongoDB. The next morning, Login → Open Daily Tracker → the backend asks MongoDB for today's assigned contacts → 15 contacts are returned and the table is already populated before the coordinator types anything.

## 10.3 Case 3 - Editing a Call Status

Changing a status from No Response to Follow-up Required follows Frontend → API → Backend → Update MongoDB → Success → UI updates. This still goes through the same API/backend/MongoDB path as any other edit, but - per Section 11 - it does not require a toast notification every time.

# 11\. Auto-Save vs. Toast Notification - Decision

Question raised: does every single cell edit in the Daily Tracker produce a toast notification? If so, the interface would feel noisy very quickly given how often coordinators edit rows.

Decision: no. For a data-entry screen like the Daily Tracker, a small, subtle auto-save indicator ("Saving..." → "Saved ✓") is used instead of a toast for routine row edits. A toast notification is reserved for larger, less frequent events only - bulk import completed, export completed, delete completed - never for every individual cell edit. This keeps the operational screens calm and fast to work in, consistent with the "consistency over creativity" motion philosophy already frozen in the Chapter 2 component library.

# 12\. Application Scope: Multi-Role Web App, Not Open Source

Extending the application to Training & Placement Officers at partner colleges does not make iPOMS "open source" - open source refers to publicly available source code, which is a separate and unrelated concept. What is actually being described is a web application with multiple user roles, which is a normal and well-supported architecture.

Decision: design the authentication and permission system from the outset to support all planned roles, each seeing only the screens relevant to them:

- Coordinator
- Team Leader
- Director
- CEO
- Training & Placement Officer (college-side, future dashboard)

# 13\. Two-Source Daily Tracker Data Model

Rather than treating Team-Leader-assigned contacts and Metadata-imported contacts as two unrelated mechanisms, the recommended flow unifies them: the Metadata Database feeds a Team Leader assignment step, which populates an Assignment Table; when the coordinator opens the Daily Tracker, assigned contacts automatically appear already loaded. If more contacts are needed, the coordinator uses Import from Metadata directly.

This gives the Daily Tracker exactly two data sources: Source 1 - Assigned Contacts (from the Team Leader via the Assignment Table) and Source 2 - Imported from Metadata (coordinator-initiated, bulk import) - matching the real operational process described for iPOMS.

# 14\. Recommended Addition - Section 4.1.1: System Data Flow

Before designing MongoDB collections in detail (Section 4.3), a small, non-technical sub-section is recommended: 4.1.1 - System Data Flow, describing only the business-level movement of data, independent of any implementation detail:

Metadata Database → Team Leader Assignment → Daily Tracker → Weekly Tracker → Daily Leads → Reports & Analytics → Dashboards.

This becomes the master flow of the application. Once frozen, designing MongoDB collections, APIs, and backend logic becomes considerably easier, because every piece of data already has a clearly defined origin and destination before any schema is written.

# 15\. Business Rules Summary

- Architecture is designed before implementation: Section 4.1 (overall system behaviour) is decided before Section 4.3 (MongoDB collections) - the database is never the starting point.
- The frontend never makes authorization or validation decisions itself; all such decisions are made by the backend.
- Bulk operations (e.g. importing 30-40 contacts) are always a single API request and a single backend validation pass, not one request per record.
- Routine row-level edits use a subtle auto-save indicator, not a toast notification; toasts are reserved for bulk import, export, and delete completions.
- MongoDB stores structured data only (users, companies, operational records); logos, Excel imports, and generated PDFs are handled as files, with PDFs downloaded to the user's device rather than retained on the server.
- iPOMS Version 1 serves a single organization (Infoziant) only - no multi-branch or multi-tenant support in this version.
- The application must support both internal office access and internet access from Version 1, since Training & Placement Officers at partner colleges will eventually need external access.
- The Daily Tracker's two data sources - Team Leader assignment and Metadata import - are both first-class, intentional pathways, not one official mechanism and one workaround.

# 16\. Terminology Clarifications

- API ≠ Internet. An API is the communication contract between frontend and backend, used identically whether the application runs on an office network or over the public internet.
- Open Source ≠ Multi-Role Application. Adding more user roles (e.g. college Training & Placement Officers) does not make software "open source" - that term refers specifically to publicly available source code.
- MongoDB is storage, not logic. All decision-making (validation, permissions, calculations) happens in backend business logic; MongoDB simply persists the result, "like memory."

# 17\. Relationship to Chapters 1-3

Every screen frozen in Chapter 3 depends on the decisions in this chapter: the Daily Tracker's inline editing and auto-save, the Master Company Database's bulk import, and the Reports & Analytics module's live regeneration from operational data all assume the API/backend/MongoDB flow described here. Chapter 4 does not redesign any screen - it defines the engine that makes the screens already designed actually work.

# 18\. Conclusion

Section 4.1 - Overall Backend Architecture is functionally framed: the system model (frontend, API, backend logic, MongoDB), the recommended technology stack, the four foundational business decisions (access mode, concurrent users, file storage, future growth), and the clarified Daily Tracker data flow are all captured above. This gives Claude Code and Cursor AI a clear instruction manual for where data should be saved, read, and validated, without requiring the AI to guess or invent its own architecture.
